The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles (the six clinical judgment steps within the PN role, insulin onset and peak with hypoglycemia watched for at peak, insulin administration).

brief.situation: 11:10 in a long-term care home. You are the LPN for the west hall. The nursing assistant calls you to Room 14: Mrs. Kowalski, 84, is sweaty and shaky and 'isn't making sense'.
handover: Type 2 diabetes on insulin: glargine 18 units at bedtime, and insulin lispro 6 units with each meal. You gave her breakfast lispro at 07:45; she was nauseated and ate about a quarter of her breakfast.
Her lunch tray comes at 11:45, and her next 6 units of lispro are due with it.

The hypoglycemia protocol (standing order): for glucose below 70 mg/dL and able to swallow, 15 g of fast carbohydrate (4 oz juice or 4 glucose tablets), recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still below 70; once above 70, a snack with protein and carbohydrate; if she cannot swallow safely, glucagon 1 mg IM and turn her on her side; tell the RN about any glucose below 70.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Recognize what is happening, act, and check whether it worked. Absorbing sugar and walking the RN to the room take a few minutes.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at 12:40 at the latest, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: FLAG: authored. Her breakfast lispro with little food keeps pulling her glucose down by about 0.5 mg/dL a minute until about 12:30. Lispro's time to peak insulin concentration is 30-90 min (Lilly); the label data give no rate of glucose fall for this situation. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. The breakfast dose stops pulling her glucose down at about 12:30, nearly five hours after it was given (Lilly gives a shorter duration than regular insulin, with no number). Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. Each gram of carbohydrate she absorbs raises her glucose about 3 mg/dL, so 15 g raises it about 45 mg/dL. No guideline gives this number; the ADA and CDC only say to recheck at 15 min. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. Juice or glucose tablets are absorbed at about a tenth of what is left each minute, about three quarters in 15 min. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. Food with fat or protein (chocolate, crackers with peanut butter, a sandwich) is absorbed about three times more slowly (CDC: fat slows how fast sugar is absorbed). Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

source.cite: Lupin. Glucagon for Injection prescribing information (March 2024), section 12.2

cues.question: What cues point to the problem, why now, what did you do, how will you know it worked, and what does the RN need to decide?

parts.label: Cues, the likely cause and why now
parts.criteria: Names sweating, trembling, a fast pulse and new confusion with a glucose below 70 as hypoglycemia; links it to her breakfast lispro with little food eaten; names the risk of another low and of the lunch dose if she eats little; does not settle on another cause (stroke, infection) without the glucose.
parts.modelAnswer: Sweating, trembling, a fast pulse and new confusion with a glucose of 58 is hypoglycemia. She had 6 units of lispro at 07:45 and ate a quarter of breakfast, so her insulin was working with little food. Until that wears off she can drop again, and the 11:45 dose with a small lunch would make it worse.

parts.label: Action, evaluation and what goes to the RN
parts.criteria: Checks the glucose and that she can swallow, gives 15 g of fast carbohydrate (juice or tablets, not chocolate), rechecks in 15 minutes and repeats below 70, gives a snack once above 70, uses glucagon only if she cannot swallow; reports to the RN and asks for the lunch insulin to be reviewed, holding it meanwhile; documents objectively.
parts.modelAnswer: Fingerstick and a swallow check, then 4 oz of juice under the protocol. Recheck at 15 minutes; if still under 70, another 15 g; once above 70, a sandwich and milk. If she couldn't swallow, glucagon IM and on her side. SBAR to the RN: treated low, little intake, please review the 11:45 lispro with the provider; I hold it until then. Document each reading and time.

noProgress.rationale: If she is out of danger at 12:40 but her insulin with poor intake never reached the RN and provider, the immediate goal was met but the cause was not, so a repeat low is likely: this case calls it recovered, not target.

expertPath.text: Go to her: sweaty, trembling, confused, can swallow. Fingerstick: 58 mg/dL.
4 oz of juice under the protocol. SBAR to the RN: treated low, little breakfast after lispro, please review the 11:45 dose. Hold it meanwhile.
Recheck at 15 minutes: above 70. Half a sandwich and milk. Objective note.
Provider: hold the lunch lispro, glucose before lunch and at 14:00, doses reviewed this afternoon.

seizure.headline: Severe hypoglycemia: a seizure
seizure.body: Sweating, shaking and confusion in someone on insulin is a low until a glucose says otherwise. Find when the glucose was checked, when 15 g went in, whether it was rechecked at 15 minutes, and whether lunch insulin went in on top of it.

aspirated.headline: Juice into a mouth that couldn't swallow
aspirated.body: Oral sugar is only for someone awake and able to swallow. When she can't, the protocol is glucagon IM and turning her on her side.

stable.headline: Recognized, treated, checked, reported
stable.body: You checked before treating, used fast sugar, rechecked at 15 minutes, followed with a real snack, and sent the cause, her insulin with poor intake, to the RN and provider. That is the expert path and every step of clinical judgment.

stableLate.headline: Safe now, by a slower route
stableLate.body: She is above 70, but check how fast you treated, what you gave, whether you rechecked at 15 minutes, and whether the lunch insulin waited for the review.

time_up.headline: Treated, but the cause stayed put
time_up.body: Treating the number is half the job. Insulin given with little food caused this; the RN and provider need to hear it so the next dose changes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Recognize cues: sweating, trembling, a fast pulse and new confusion in a resident on insulin. Analyze: she had lispro at 07:45 and ate a quarter of breakfast, so insulin is working with little food. Prioritize: hypoglycemia first, confirmed by a fingerstick (58 mg/dL), over other causes of confusion. Generate solutions and act: she can swallow, so 15 g of fast carbohydrate (4 oz juice or glucose tablets) under the protocol, not chocolate or crackers, whose fat slows absorption; glucagon IM and side-lying only if she cannot swallow. Evaluate: recheck in 15 minutes, repeat below 70, and once above 70 give a snack with protein and carbohydrate. Report what needs RN judgment: the low, her intake and the lunch lispro, held until the RN and provider review it. Document each reading and time.

fatQ.ask: While the RN comes: why not the chocolate bar from the station?

choices.label: Its fat slows how fast the sugar gets in
It works just as well as juice

fatQ.explain: CDC: foods high in fat, such as chocolate, slow down how fast sugar is absorbed. Use 4 oz of juice or glucose tablets, then a balanced snack once she is back up.
